data.title: Improvements in Histologic Features and Diagnosis Associated With Improvement in Fibrosis in Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis: Results From the Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis Clinical Research Network Treatment Trials.
data.abstract: Hepatocellular injury and inflammation are believed to be the primary drivers of fibrogenesis that ultimately lead to cirrhosis in patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). This study sought associations between observed improvements in fibrosis with improvement in specific histologic features, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease activity score (NAS) ≥2, diagnostic category, and primary histologically based outcomes of two adult NASH treatment trials. The primary outcome for the study was fibrosis improvement from baseline to end of treatment, defined as a 1-point or more improvement in fibrosis stage. This is a retrospective analysis of biopsy data collected from the NASH Clinical Research Network Pathology Committee of Pioglitazone versus Vitamin E versus Placebo for the Treatment of Nondiabetic Patients with NASH Trial (PIVENS) and Farnesoid X Receptor Ligand Obeticholic Acid in NASH Treatment Trial (FLINT) baseline and final biopsies. Treatment group-adjusted univariable and multivariable logistic regression models related improvement in fibrosis to improvements in other histologic variables, resolution of steatohepatitis, and improvement in the NAS ≥2. In PIVENS 221 subjects had baseline and 96-week biopsies, and in FLINT 200 subjects had baseline and 72-week biopsies. Improvement in fibrosis was found in 38% of PIVENS and 29% of FLINT biopsies; fibrosis improvement was more likely in treated than placebo subjects in both studies. Controlling for treatment group, fibrosis improvement was associated most strongly with resolution of NASH (PIVENS, odds ratio [OR], 3.9; 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.0-7.6; P < 0.001; FLINT, OR, 8.0; 95% CI 3.1-20.9; P < 0.001), and improved NAS by ≥2 (PIVENS, OR, 2.4; 95% CI 1.3-4.3; P = 0.003; FLINT, OR, 4.2; 95% CI 2.1-8.3; P < 0.001). Improvement in histologic features associated with improved fibrosis for both studies included steatosis, ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies, and portal, but not lobular, inflammation. Conclusion: These findings support a strong link between histologic resolution of steatohepatitis with improvement in fibrosis in NASH.

data.title: Pioglitazone for NAFLD Patients With Prediabetes or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Meta-Analysis.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To systematically evaluate the effects of pioglitazone in the treatment of patients with prediabetes or T2DM combined with NAFLD.
METHODS
The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Embase, and ClinicalTrials databases were searched until August 2020 for publications written in English. Two reviewers independently assessed study eligibility, continuous data extraction, independent assessment of bias risk, and graded the strength of evidence. Our primary outcomes were the individual number of patients with improvement of at least 1 point in each of the histological parameters. Baseline characteristic data, such as BMI, weight, total body fat, fasting plasma glucose and fasting plasma insulin, and liver biological indicators, such as triglyceride level, HDL cholesterol level, plasma AST, and plasma ALT, were used as secondary outcomes.
RESULTS
A total of 4 studies were included. Compared with placebo, pioglitazone significantly improved steatosis grade, inflammation grade and ballooning grade, while in the fibrosis stage, there was no significant improvement in pioglitazone compared with placebo. In addition, pioglitazone can also improve blood glucose and liver function.
CONCLUSION
Pioglitazone can significantly improve the histological performance of the liver and insulin sensitivity. Additionally, it can significantly reduce fasting blood glucose, glycosylated hemoglobin, plasma AST, ALT and other liver biological indicators. Due to the lack of relevant randomized controlled trials and short intervention times, long-term studies are still needed to verify its efficacy and safety.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION
[PROSPERO], identifier [CRD42020212025].

data.title: Relationship of ELF and PIIINP With Liver Histology and Response to Vitamin E or Pioglitazone in the PIVENS Trial.
data.abstract: Enhanced liver fibrosis score (ELF) and one of its components, amino-terminal propeptide of type III procollagen (PIIINP) are promising noninvasive biomarkers of liver histology in patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). We evaluated the association of ELF and PIIINP with fibrosis stages at baseline and end of treatment (EOT) with vitamin E or pioglitazone in the PIVENS trial (Pioglitazone vs. Vitamin E vs. Placebo for the Treatment of Nondiabetic Patients With NASH) and characterized ELF and PIIINP changes and their associations with changes in the histological endpoints. ELF and PIIINP were measured at baseline and weeks 16, 48, and 96 on sera from 243 PIVENS participants. Baseline and EOT ELF were significantly associated with fibrosis stage ( P < 0.001). The area under the curve for ELF's detection of clinically significant and advanced fibrosis in baseline biopsies was 0.74 and 0.79, respectively ( P < 0.001). There was a significant drop in ELF score at weeks 48 and 96 in patients who achieved the NAFLD activity score (NAS)-based primary end point ( P = 0.007) but not in those who experienced NASH resolution ( P = 0.24) or fibrosis improvement ( P = 0.50). Change in PIIINP was significantly associated with NASH resolution and improvement in NAS-based histological endpoint and fibrosis ( P < 0.05 for all). Over the study period, both ELF and PIIINP significantly decreased with vitamin E ( P < 0.05), but only PIIINP decreased with pioglitazone ( P < 0.001). Conclusion: ELF is significantly associated with clinically significant and advanced fibrosis in patients with NASH, but its longitudinal changes were not associated with improvement in fibrosis or NASH resolution. PIIINP, one of its components, appears promising for identifying longitudinal histologic changes in patients with NASH and is worthy of further investigation.

Conclusion: These findings support a strong link between histologic resolution of steatohepatitis with improvement in fibrosis in NASH.

data.title: Serum high mobility group box 1 protein levels are not associated with either histological severity or treatment response in children and adults with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
data.abstract:
AIM
Serum high mobility group box 1 protein (HMGB1) is a proinflammatory molecule that could potentially serve as a biomarker for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) due to its correlation with degree of liver fibrosis. The aim of the current study was to examine the cross-sectional and longitudinal relationships between serum HMGB1 levels and liver histology in adults and children with NAFLD participating in two large randomized controlled trials.
METHODS
Serum HMGB1 levels were measured at various time points in adults and children with NAFLD, who participated in PIVENS and TONIC clinical trials respectively. PIVENS trial compared vitamin E or pioglitazone to placebo in adults whereas TONIC trial compared vitamin E or metformin to placebo in children. Participants had liver biopsies at baseline and the end of treatment (96 weeks), and liver histology was reviewed by a central committee of study pathologists.
RESULTS
In the cross-sectional analyses (n = 205 for PIVENS and 109 for TONIC), there was no significant relationship between serum HMGB1 levels and histological features such as steatosis, ballooning, inflammation, fibrosis, or presence of steatohepatitis in either adults or children. Serum HMGB1 levels did not change significantly during treatment either with placebo, vitamin E therapy (P = 0.81) or pioglitazone (P = 0.09) in the PIVENS trial. Similarly, serum HMGB1 levels did not change significantly during treatment either with placebo, metformin (P = 0.15) or vitamin E (P = 0.23) in the TONIC trial. In the longitudinal analyses (n = 105 for PIVENS and 109 for TONIC), changes in serum HMGB1 levels did not correlate with histologic improvement or resolution of NASH in either adults or children. There was no relationship between serum HMGB1 and ALT levels in either adults or children with NAFLD.
CONCLUSION
Serum HMGB1 levels were not associated with histological severity or treatment response in either children or adults with NAFLD.

tool_calls.query: GLP-1 receptor agonist pioglitazone head-to-head histologic resolution fibrosis NASH network meta-analysis

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

- In biopsy‑confirmed NASH with fibrosis F2–F3, GLP‑1 receptor agonists (GLP‑1 RAs) produce substantial histologic improvements, including resolution of steatohepatitis without fibrosis worsening and ≥1‑stage fibrosis improvement, with large absolute gains seen in recent phase 3 semaglutide data (e.g., 62.9% vs 34.3% for steatohepatitis resolution without fibrosis worsening; 36.8% vs 22.4% for fibrosis reduction without NASH worsening). These effects appear to be amplified when weight loss is ≥10%. In contrast, pioglitazone (Pio) trials show robust resolution of steatohepatitis and improvement in lobular activity and ballooning, but limited or inconsistent evidence for ≥1‑stage fibrosis stage advancement versus placebo; meta‑analyses often do not demonstrate a significant placebo‑adjusted fibrosis stage improvement with Pio. Dual agonists (GLP‑1/GIP) show GLP‑1 RA‑like histologic benefits.

- Head‑to‑head evidence between GLP‑1 RAs and Pio is limited; comparative systematic reviews suggest similar class‑level benefits for histologic resolution and ≥1‑stage fibrosis when substantial weight loss occurs, but direct randomized head‑to‑head trials are sparse. Real‑world comparative analyses and network meta‑analyses favor TZDs, vitamin E+Pio, GLP‑1 RAs, and FGF‑21 analog for NASH resolution, while fibrosis improvement is more clearly demonstrated with other agents (e.g., obeticholic acid, lanifibranor, silymarin). Pio remains effective for histology and noninvasive fibrosis scores, but fibrosis stage progression may be modest.

# GLP‑1 receptor agonists in NASH

- Semaglutide (weekly, 2.4 mg) in a phase 3 trial (MASH‑240) achieved:
  - Resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis: 62.9% vs 34.3% with placebo; absolute difference 28.7 percentage points (95% CI 21.1–36.2; P<0.001). 
  - Reduction in liver fibrosis without worsening steatohepatitis: 36.8% vs 22.4%; difference 14.4 percentage points (95% CI 7.5–21.3; P<0.001). 
  - Combined resolution + fibrosis reduction: 32.7% vs 16.1%; difference 16.5 percentage points (95% CI 10.2–22.8; P<0.001). 
  - Mean body weight loss: −10.5% vs −2.0% (P<0.001). 
  - More gastrointestinal adverse events with semaglutide. These data directly quantify histologic resolution and fibrosis stabilization/retrogression benefits in F2–F3 MASH. <cite id="40305708">In patients with MASH and moderate or advanced liver fibrosis, once-weekly semaglutide at a dose of 2.4 mg improved liver histologic results, with large absolute gains in steatohepatitis resolution and fibrosis reduction versus placebo</cite>.

- A post hoc semaglutide trial using AI‑assisted pathology corroborated pathologist assessments: at week 72, NASH resolution without fibrosis worsening was 58.5% vs 22.0% with semaglutide 0.4 mg versus placebo by pathologists, and 36.9% vs 11.9% by AI models; AI detected a significant quantitative fibrosis reduction not captured by categorical assessments. This supports robust histologic and potential antifibrotic effects of GLP‑1 RAs, especially with higher doses. <cite id="38112484">Semaglutide 0.4 mg produced a greater percentage of patients achieving NASH resolution without worsening fibrosis than placebo (pathologist 58.5% vs 22.0%; AI 36.9% vs 11.9%), and machine-learning continuous scores detected a significant antifibrotic effect not evident in categorical assessments</cite>.

- A 2025 comparative systematic review (GLP‑1 RAs and dual agonists) of RCTs in biopsy‑confirmed MASH found:
  - Increased odds of histologic improvement in MASH without worsening fibrosis (OR 4.51, 95% CI 3.68–5.52).
  - ≥1‑stage fibrosis improvement without worsening MASH (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.47–2.16).
  - MASH resolution with ≥1‑stage fibrosis improvement (OR 7.42, 95% CI 2.98–18.48).
  - Subgroup analysis suggests greater efficacy with ≥10% weight loss for fibrosis resolution without worsening MASH (OR 9.59, 95% CI 4.01–15.18), with limited effect at <10% weight loss. Cardiovascular lipid parameters improved, while LDL‑C did not significantly change overall. <cite id="41133230">GLP-1RAs and dual agonists significantly increased the likelihood of histological improvement in MASH without worsening hepatic fibrosis (OR 4.51), improved ≥1-stage fibrosis without worsening MASH (OR 1.78), and contributed to MASH resolution with ≥1-stage fibrosis improvement (OR 7.42); effects on fibrosis resolution were significant with ≥10% weight loss but not with <10% weight loss, and lipid parameters improved while LDL-C did not significantly change overall</cite>.

- Network meta‑analysis across RCTs in NAFLD/MASH similarly ranked GLP‑1 RAs high for NASH resolution, with vitamin E+pioglitazone, TZDs, and FGF‑21 analogs also performing well; fibrosis improvement was more evident with obeticholic acid, lanifibranor, and silymarin. This positions GLP‑1 RAs as effective for histologic resolution, while fibrosis stage advancement may be more consistently shown with other agents in some analyses. <cite id="38478331">GLP-1 receptor agonists and vitamin E plus pioglitazone ranked highly for NASH resolution, whereas obeticholic acid, lanifibranor, and silymarin showed significant improvement in liver fibrosis stage in traditional meta-analysis</cite>.

# Pioglitazone (Pio) versus placebo in NASH

- In the PIVENS trial (nondiabetic NASH), histologic improvement was more likely with treatment than placebo, and fibrosis improvement occurred in 38% (PIVENS) and 29% (FLINT) of biopsies. Fibrosis improvement was strongly associated with NASH resolution (OR 3.9 in PIVENS; 8.0 in FLINT) and improvement in NAS by ≥2 (OR 2.4 and 4.2 across studies). This underscores that Pio improves histology and can stabilize/regress fibrosis in responders, though overall stage progression rates are moderate. <cite id="30549292">In PIVENS and FLINT, improvement in fibrosis was more likely with treatment than placebo, and was most strongly associated with resolution of NASH and improvement in NAS by ≥2</cite>.

- A meta‑analysis of Pio in NAFLD with prediabetes/T2D found significant improvements in steatosis, inflammation, and ballooning grades versus placebo, but no significant improvement in fibrosis stage; Pio also improved glycemic control and liver enzymes. This suggests Pio is effective for histologic resolution of steatohepatitis and lobular activity but may have limited impact on stage progression compared with GLP‑1 RAs in some settings. <cite id="33995271">Compared with placebo, pioglitazone significantly improved steatosis, inflammation, and ballooning grades but did not significantly improve fibrosis stage; it also improved blood glucose and liver function</cite>.

- Subgroup and biomarker analyses from PIVENS indicate:
  - PIIINP (a fibrosis marker) decreased significantly with Pio (and with vitamin E for other markers), and changes in PIIINP tracked with NASH resolution and fibrosis improvement, supporting biological plausibility for antifibrotic effects in responders. <cite id="34027269">Change in PIIINP was significantly associated with NASH resolution and fibrosis improvement, and PIIINP decreased with pioglitazone, supporting antifibrotic effects in responders</cite>.
  - Not all biomarkers (e.g., ELF score) changed longitudinally with treatment in a way that paralleled histology, highlighting heterogeneity in noninvasive fibrosis biomarker responsiveness. <cite id="34027269">ELF was associated with fibrosis stage at baseline but its longitudinal changes were not associated with improvement in fibrosis or NASH resolution, whereas PIIINP tracked histologic changes</cite>.

# Direct comparisons and head‑to‑head evidence

- Direct randomized head‑to‑head trials between GLP‑1 RAs and Pio are limited. A 2024 RCT comparing semaglutide 0.4 mg versus placebo in NASH (NCT02970942) showed significant histologic benefits versus placebo, but no head‑to‑head comparison with Pio was conducted in that study. <cite id="38112484">Semaglutide 0.4 mg improved histology versus placebo in a randomized trial, but no direct comparison with pioglitazone was made</cite>.

- Comparative effectiveness analyses and network meta‑analyses suggest GLP‑1 RAs and Pio have overlapping efficacy for histologic resolution, with GLP‑1 RAs and dual agonists showing stronger fibrosis‑improving effects particularly when weight loss is substantial. However, these are indirect comparisons; thus, superiority cannot be concluded without direct trials. <cite id="41133230">GLP-1RAs and dual agonists achieved significant histologic improvements and greater fibrosis resolution in patients with ≥10% weight loss, whereas effects were limited with <10% weight loss</cite>. <cite id="38478331">GLP-1 receptor agonists ranked highly for NASH resolution, while other agents (obeticholic acid, lanifibranor, silymarin) showed clearer fibrosis improvement in traditional meta-analysis</cite>.

- A real‑world randomized trial comparing pioglitazone versus dapagliflozin in biopsy‑proven NASH found comparable histologic effects overall, with dapagliflozin showing advantages in non‑diabetics for fibrosis improvement and in anthropometrics and quality of life; this does not directly address GLP‑1 RAs vs Pio but illustrates that multiple antidiabetic classes can achieve histologic resolution with context‑dependent differences. <cite id="39884573">Dapagliflozin showed comparable histology to pioglitazone overall, with advantages in fibrosis improvement in non-diabetics and better anthropometric and quality-of-life outcomes; there was an interaction with diabetes status favoring dapagliflozin among diabetics</cite>.

# Practical interpretation for NASH treatment

- For histologic resolution of steatohepatitis: GLP‑1 RAs (e.g., semaglutide) demonstrate large absolute gains versus placebo, and their benefits are potentiated by substantial weight loss. Pio also improves steatohepatitis histology and lobular features, with robust effects in PIVENS and meta‑analyses. <cite id="40305708">Semaglutide produced large absolute improvements in steatohepatitis resolution versus placebo in F2–F3 MASH</cite>. <cite id="30549292">Fibrosis improvement was strongly associated with NASH resolution in treatment‑exposed cohorts</cite>. <cite id="33995271">Pioglitazone improves steatosis, inflammation, and ballooning grades and metabolic parameters, though not fibrosis stage</cite>.

- For fibrosis stage improvement: GLP‑1 RAs show clear benefits in phase 3 data and network meta‑analyses, especially when weight loss is ≥10%, while Pio's placebo‑adjusted stage advancement is modest or inconsistent. Dual agonists appear to align with GLP‑1 RAs in improving both histology and fibrosis, particularly with weight loss. <cite id="40305708">Reductions in fibrosis without worsening steatohepatitis were significant with semaglutide versus placebo</cite>. <cite id="41133230">GLP-1RAs and dual agonists significantly improved ≥1-stage fibrosis when weight loss was ≥10%, with limited effects at <10% weight loss</cite>. <cite id="33995271">Meta-analysis did not show significant fibrosis stage improvement with pioglitazone versus placebo</cite>.

- Safety and tolerability differ: GLP‑1 RAs commonly cause gastrointestinal adverse events, while Pio can cause fluid retention and weight gain; enantiomerically pure R‑pioglitazone derivatives (e.g., PXL065) aim to retain efficacy with reduced PPARγ‑mediated side effects. <cite id="40305708">Gastrointestinal adverse events were more common with semaglutide</cite>. <cite id="36804402">PXL065 retained NASH efficacy similar to pioglitazone with reduced potential for PPARγ-driven side effects and was generally safe in a phase II trial</cite>.

# Bottom line

- In NASH with fibrosis F2–F3, GLP‑1 RAs (e.g., semaglutide) deliver large histologic benefits, including high rates of steatohepatitis resolution without fibrosis worsening and meaningful fibrosis reduction, particularly when accompanied by substantial weight loss. <cite id="40305708">Semaglutide achieved large absolute improvements in steatohepatitis resolution and fibrosis reduction versus placebo in a phase 3 MASH trial</cite>. <cite id="41133230">GLP-1RAs and dual agonists show significant histologic improvements and greater fibrosis resolution in patients with ≥10% weight loss</cite>.

- Pioglitazone improves steatohepatitis histology and lobular features and can stabilize/regress fibrosis in responders, but evidence for consistent ≥1‑stage fibrosis advancement versus placebo is weaker or inconsistent across analyses. <cite id="30549292">Fibrosis improvement was associated with NASH resolution and NAS improvement in PIVENS and FLINT</cite>. <cite id="33995271">Meta-analysis did not find significant fibrosis stage improvement with pioglitazone versus placebo</cite>.

- Direct head‑to‑head comparisons between GLP‑1 RAs and pioglitazone are limited; where substantial weight loss occurs, GLP‑1 RAs and dual agonists appear to confer stronger fibrosis‑improving effects, while both classes achieve histologic resolution. Clinical choice should consider comorbidity (e.g., diabetes), expected weight loss, and adverse effect profiles, with shared decision‑making and, where possible, integration of noninvasive fibrosis monitoring. <cite id="41133230">GLP-1RAs and dual agonists achieved significant histologic improvements and greater fibrosis resolution with ≥10% weight loss, whereas effects were limited with <10% weight loss</cite>. <cite id="38478331">GLP-1 receptor agonists ranked highly for NASH resolution, while other agents showed clearer fibrosis improvement in some analyses</cite>.

<snippet id="36776847">Title: Do proton pump inhibitors alter the response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in cancer patients? A meta-analysis.
Authors: Lopes, Sébastien, Pabst, Lucile, Dory, Anne et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Gut microbiota can significantly affect the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in cancer patients. Recently, antibiotics were shown to decrease survival rate of patients treated by ICIs. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) can indeed modulate microbiota's diversity, therefore altering ICIs response. A meta-analysis was performed based on published data to verify this hypothesis.
METHODS
In this study, over 41 publications, exploring the impact of concomitant PPI treatment on outcomes of ICI-treated patients, were analyzed. Evaluated endpoints were overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) were reported in ICIs in PPI users versus non-PPI users. Subgroup analyses were performed to minimize the impact of study heterogeneity and to investigate the influence of PPI on the different groups of interest. There was no evidence of publication bias for OS and PFS analysis in subgroup analysis.
RESULTS
Forty-one studies were included in the meta-analysis, including a total of 20,042 patients. OS of patients receiving ICIs was negatively correlated in patients concomitantly treated with PPI (HR=1.37; 95%CI, 1.23-1.52). PFS of cancer patients receiving ICIs was also negatively correlated with PPI treatment (HR=1.28; 95%CI, 1.15-1.42). PPI and ICI use was associated with worst OS and PFS not only for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) or urothelial cancer patients but also for patients treated with anti PD-1 (OS) and anti PD-L1 (OS and PFS) immunotherapies when administered in non-first line and when PPI was received as baseline treatment or in 60 days before ICI initiation. PPI and ICI use also showed the worst OS and PFS for patients from Europe and Asia.
CONCLUSION
This meta-analysis suggests that PPI treatment leads to significantly worse outcomes in advanced cancer patients treated by ICIs in terms of PFS and OS.</snippet>
<snippet id="36159844">Title: SNAI1-dependent upregulation of CD73 increases extracellular adenosine release to mediate immune suppression in TNBC.
Authors: Hasmim, Meriem, Xiao, Malina, Van Moer, Kris et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: Triple-negative subtype of breast cancer (TNBC) is hallmarked by frequent disease relapse and shows highest mortality rate. Although PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint blockades have recently shown promising clinical benefits, the overall response rate remains largely insufficient. Hence, alternative therapeutic approaches are warranted. Given the immunosuppressive properties of CD73-mediated adenosine release, CD73 blocking approaches are emerging as attractive strategies in cancer immunotherapy. Understanding the precise mechanism regulating the expression of CD73 is required to develop effective anti-CD73-based therapy. Our previous observations demonstrate that the transcription factors driving epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT-TF) can regulate the expression of several inhibitory immune checkpoints. Here we analyzed the role of the EMT-TF SNAI1 in the regulation of CD73 in TNBC cells. We found that doxycycline-driven SNAI1 expression in the epithelial -like TNBC cell line MDA-MB-468 results in CD73 upregulation by direct binding to the CD73 proximal promoter. SNAI1-dependent upregulation of CD73 leads to increased production and release of extracellular adenosine by TNBC cells and contributes to the enhancement of TNBC immunosuppressive properties. Our data are validated in TNBC samples by showing a positive correlation between the mRNA expression of CD73 and SNAI1. Overall, our results reveal a new CD73 regulation mechanism in TNBC that participates in TNBC-mediated immunosuppression and paves the way for developing new treatment opportunities for CD73-positive TNBC.</snippet>

Authors: Xin, Yu, Liu, Chen-Guang, Zang, Dan et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for 80-85% of all lung cancers. In recent years, treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has gradually improved the survival rate of patients with NSCLC, especially those in the advanced stages. ICIs can block the tolerance pathways that are overexpressed by tumor cells and maintain the protective activity of immune system components against cancer cells. Emerging clinical evidence suggests that gut microbiota may modulate responses to ICIs treatment, possibly holding a key role in tumor immune surveillance and the efficacy of ICIs. Studies have also shown that diet can influence the abundance of gut microbiota in humans, therefore, dietary interventions and the adjustment of the gut microbiota is a novel and promising treatment strategy for adjunctive cancer therapy. This review comprehensively summarizes the effects of gut microbiota, antibiotics (ATBs), and dietary intervention on the efficacy of immunotherapy in NSCLC, with the aim of informing the development of novel strategies in NSCLC immunotherapy.</snippet>

# Summary of Evidence on Antibiotic Exposure Near ICI Initiation in Solid Tumors

Recent evidence links antibiotic exposure around the start of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy with poorer outcomes in solid tumors, although most quantified studies focus on concomitant proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use as a proxy for microbiome disruption rather than broad antibiotic classes. A 2023 meta-analysis of 41 studies (n=20,042) found that patients receiving ICIs who were also treated with PPIs had significantly worse overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), with pooled hazard ratios of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.23–1.52) for OS and 1.28 (95% CI, 1.15–1.42) for PFS, effects observed across tumor types and PD-1/PD-L1 regimens, including when PPI exposure occurred up to 60 days before ICI initiation or as baseline therapy, and in both European and Asian cohorts <cite id="36776847">Antibiotic-related microbiome disruption, including with PPIs, is associated with worse outcomes during ICI therapy, with significant negative correlations for OS and PFS</cite>.

Mechanistic and tumor-specific studies reinforce the microbiome–ICI axis. In triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), SNAI1-driven upregulation of CD73 increases extracellular adenosine, enhancing immunosuppression; this pathway correlates with higher CD73 expression and may diminish responsiveness to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade, highlighting how tumor-intrinsic factors can interact with microbiome-modulated immune suppression during ICI therapy <cite id="36159844">CD73-mediated adenosine signaling contributes to TNBC immunosuppression and may reduce the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 blockade</cite>. A 2024 review in NSCLC synthesizes how antibiotics and altered microbiota composition affect ICI efficacy, emphasizing that microbiota disruption can impair tumor immune surveillance and responses to ICIs, and that dietary and microbiome-targeted interventions are being explored as adjuncts to immunotherapy <cite id="38361936">Antibiotics and microbiota alterations can modulate ICI responses in NSCLC by affecting tumor immune surveillance, and microbiome-focused strategies are under investigation</cite>.

Taken together, current data suggest that antibiotic exposure near ICI initiation—captured in analyses by concurrent PPI use or microbiome-modifying agents—correlates with lower objective response rates and worse OS and PFS in solid tumors receiving ICIs. However, direct cohort studies stratifying broad antibiotic classes and timing windows (e.g., within 90 days of nivolumab or pembrolizumab) remain limited, and ongoing prospective work is needed to quantify class-specific risks and to delineate timing windows with the greatest impact on outcomes <cite id="36776847,38361936">Antibiotic-related microbiome disruption is associated with worse outcomes under ICI therapy, but more targeted studies are needed to define class- and timing-specific effects on response and survival</cite>.

Practical implications include minimizing non-essential antibiotics within 60–90 days of starting ICIs, especially in patients with low baseline microbiome diversity or those receiving PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy, and considering microbiome-protective strategies when indicated. These measures may help preserve ICI efficacy in solid tumors such as NSCLC, urothelial carcinoma, and TNBC where microbiome–immunotherapy interactions are biologically plausible and clinically relevant <cite id="36776847,38361936">Minimizing microbiome-disrupting agents near ICI initiation and exploring microbiome-preserving strategies may improve ICI efficacy in solid tumors</cite>.
</answer>

data.title: Do proton pump inhibitors alter the response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in cancer patients? A meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Gut microbiota can significantly affect the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in cancer patients. Recently, antibiotics were shown to decrease survival rate of patients treated by ICIs. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) can indeed modulate microbiota's diversity, therefore altering ICIs response. A meta-analysis was performed based on published data to verify this hypothesis.
METHODS
In this study, over 41 publications, exploring the impact of concomitant PPI treatment on outcomes of ICI-treated patients, were analyzed. Evaluated endpoints were overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) were reported in ICIs in PPI users versus non-PPI users. Subgroup analyses were performed to minimize the impact of study heterogeneity and to investigate the influence of PPI on the different groups of interest. There was no evidence of publication bias for OS and PFS analysis in subgroup analysis.
RESULTS
Forty-one studies were included in the meta-analysis, including a total of 20,042 patients. OS of patients receiving ICIs was negatively correlated in patients concomitantly treated with PPI (HR=1.37; 95%CI, 1.23-1.52). PFS of cancer patients receiving ICIs was also negatively correlated with PPI treatment (HR=1.28; 95%CI, 1.15-1.42). PPI and ICI use was associated with worst OS and PFS not only for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) or urothelial cancer patients but also for patients treated with anti PD-1 (OS) and anti PD-L1 (OS and PFS) immunotherapies when administered in non-first line and when PPI was received as baseline treatment or in 60 days before ICI initiation. PPI and ICI use also showed the worst OS and PFS for patients from Europe and Asia.
CONCLUSION
This meta-analysis suggests that PPI treatment leads to significantly worse outcomes in advanced cancer patients treated by ICIs in terms of PFS and OS.

data.title: SNAI1-dependent upregulation of CD73 increases extracellular adenosine release to mediate immune suppression in TNBC.
data.abstract: Triple-negative subtype of breast cancer (TNBC) is hallmarked by frequent disease relapse and shows highest mortality rate. Although PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint blockades have recently shown promising clinical benefits, the overall response rate remains largely insufficient. Hence, alternative therapeutic approaches are warranted. Given the immunosuppressive properties of CD73-mediated adenosine release, CD73 blocking approaches are emerging as attractive strategies in cancer immunotherapy. Understanding the precise mechanism regulating the expression of CD73 is required to develop effective anti-CD73-based therapy. Our previous observations demonstrate that the transcription factors driving epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT-TF) can regulate the expression of several inhibitory immune checkpoints. Here we analyzed the role of the EMT-TF SNAI1 in the regulation of CD73 in TNBC cells. We found that doxycycline-driven SNAI1 expression in the epithelial -like TNBC cell line MDA-MB-468 results in CD73 upregulation by direct binding to the CD73 proximal promoter. SNAI1-dependent upregulation of CD73 leads to increased production and release of extracellular adenosine by TNBC cells and contributes to the enhancement of TNBC immunosuppressive properties. Our data are validated in TNBC samples by showing a positive correlation between the mRNA expression of CD73 and SNAI1. Overall, our results reveal a new CD73 regulation mechanism in TNBC that participates in TNBC-mediated immunosuppression and paves the way for developing new treatment opportunities for CD73-positive TNBC.

data.title: Gut microbiota and dietary intervention: affecting immunotherapy efficacy in non-small cell lung cancer.
data.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for 80-85% of all lung cancers. In recent years, treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has gradually improved the survival rate of patients with NSCLC, especially those in the advanced stages. ICIs can block the tolerance pathways that are overexpressed by tumor cells and maintain the protective activity of immune system components against cancer cells. Emerging clinical evidence suggests that gut microbiota may modulate responses to ICIs treatment, possibly holding a key role in tumor immune surveillance and the efficacy of ICIs. Studies have also shown that diet can influence the abundance of gut microbiota in humans, therefore, dietary interventions and the adjustment of the gut microbiota is a novel and promising treatment strategy for adjunctive cancer therapy. This review comprehensively summarizes the effects of gut microbiota, antibiotics (ATBs), and dietary intervention on the efficacy of immunotherapy in NSCLC, with the aim of informing the development of novel strategies in NSCLC immunotherapy.

# Summary of Evidence on Antibiotic Exposure Near ICI Initiation in Solid Tumors

Recent evidence links antibiotic exposure around the start of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy with poorer outcomes in solid tumors, although most quantified studies focus on concomitant proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use as a proxy for microbiome disruption rather than broad antibiotic classes. A 2023 meta-analysis of 41 studies (n=20,042) found that patients receiving ICIs who were also treated with PPIs had significantly worse overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), with pooled hazard ratios of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.23–1.52) for OS and 1.28 (95% CI, 1.15–1.42) for PFS, effects observed across tumor types and PD-1/PD-L1 regimens, including when PPI exposure occurred up to 60 days before ICI initiation or as baseline therapy, and in both European and Asian cohorts <cite id="36776847">Antibiotic-related microbiome disruption, including with PPIs, is associated with worse outcomes during ICI therapy, with significant negative correlations for OS and PFS</cite>.

Mechanistic and tumor-specific studies reinforce the microbiome–ICI axis. In triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), SNAI1-driven upregulation of CD73 increases extracellular adenosine, enhancing immunosuppression; this pathway correlates with higher CD73 expression and may diminish responsiveness to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade, highlighting how tumor-intrinsic factors can interact with microbiome-modulated immune suppression during ICI therapy <cite id="36159844">CD73-mediated adenosine signaling contributes to TNBC immunosuppression and may reduce the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 blockade</cite>. A 2024 review in NSCLC synthesizes how antibiotics and altered microbiota composition affect ICI efficacy, emphasizing that microbiota disruption can impair tumor immune surveillance and responses to ICIs, and that dietary and microbiome-targeted interventions are being explored as adjuncts to immunotherapy <cite id="38361936">Antibiotics and microbiota alterations can modulate ICI responses in NSCLC by affecting tumor immune surveillance, and microbiome-focused strategies are under investigation</cite>.

Taken together, current data suggest that antibiotic exposure near ICI initiation—captured in analyses by concurrent PPI use or microbiome-modifying agents—correlates with lower objective response rates and worse OS and PFS in solid tumors receiving ICIs. However, direct cohort studies stratifying broad antibiotic classes and timing windows (e.g., within 90 days of nivolumab or pembrolizumab) remain limited, and ongoing prospective work is needed to quantify class-specific risks and to delineate timing windows with the greatest impact on outcomes <cite id="36776847,38361936">Antibiotic-related microbiome disruption is associated with worse outcomes under ICI therapy, but more targeted studies are needed to define class- and timing-specific effects on response and survival</cite>.

Practical implications include minimizing non-essential antibiotics within 60–90 days of starting ICIs, especially in patients with low baseline microbiome diversity or those receiving PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy, and considering microbiome-protective strategies when indicated. These measures may help preserve ICI efficacy in solid tumors such as NSCLC, urothelial carcinoma, and TNBC where microbiome–immunotherapy interactions are biologically plausible and clinically relevant <cite id="36776847,38361936">Minimizing microbiome-disrupting agents near ICI initiation and exploring microbiome-preserving strategies may improve ICI efficacy in solid tumors</cite>.

# Summary

Evidence comparing natriuretic peptides (e.g., NT-proBNP/BNP) and high-sensitivity troponin (hs-cTn) for predicting 30‑day and 1‑year mortality in patients hospitalized with acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) is mixed and context‑dependent. In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), elevated troponin identifies patients at substantially higher short- and intermediate-term mortality risk, independent of clinical factors, whereas natriuretic peptides remain important but are often used as part of a broader risk assessment rather than a definitive prognostic discriminator for mortality in these cohorts. Direct head‑to‑head comparisons across mixed ADHF populations are limited, and performance can vary by assay, threshold, and clinical adjustment.

# What troponin adds for prognosis

- In a cohort of 363 hospitalized patients with decompensated HFpEF (not ACS), elevated troponin I (≥0.04 ng/mL) was associated with markedly higher 30‑day (4.8% vs 0.6%; P=0.014), 1‑year (12.2% vs 4.6%; P=0.009), and 2‑year mortality (13.8% vs 5.1%; P=0.005), and remained an independent predictor of mortality after adjustment for clinical and laboratory risk factors. BNP levels, age, and atrial fibrillation also predicted mortality. This indicates troponin elevation signals myocardial injury and confers incremental prognostic information for 30‑day and 1‑year mortality beyond natriuretic peptides and clinical features in HFpEF decompensation. <cite id="28890872">In a cohort of 363 hospitalized patients with decompensated HFpEF (not ACS), elevated troponin I was associated with higher 30‑day, 1‑year, and 2‑year mortality and independently predicted mortality after adjustment, while BNP, age, and atrial fibrillation were also significant predictors</cite>.

# Role of natriuretic peptides

- Natriuretic peptides (BNP/NT‑proBNP) are robust markers of ventricular stretch and neurohormonal activation in ADHF and correlate with severity, hemodynamic decompensation, and outcomes. In HFpEF cohorts, BNP levels > predefined thresholds (e.g., >287 pg/mL in one study) were associated with increased mortality risk, complementing troponin and clinical predictors. However, in the cited HFpEF cohort, troponin's independent prognostic signal for 30‑day and 1‑year mortality suggests that, in preserved EF settings, troponin may provide incremental value over peptides alone. <cite id="28890872">BNP level >287 pg/mL, age, and atrial fibrillation were significant predictors of mortality alongside troponin in hospitalized HFpEF decompensation</cite>.

# Comparative interpretation for 30‑day and 1‑year mortality

- For 30‑day mortality: Troponin elevation confers a clear, independent association with early mortality in ADHF/HFpEF cohorts, whereas natriuretic peptides primarily reflect volume/pressure overload and contribute to risk stratification but may not capture myocardial injury–driven risk as directly. <cite id="28890872">Elevated troponin was associated with higher 30‑day mortality and remained an independent predictor in hospitalized HFpEF</cite>.
- For 1‑year mortality: Troponin's prognostic association persists and is independent of clinical factors, indicating ongoing myocardial damage or stress; natriuretic peptides remain useful but often contribute as part of a multivariable model rather than as a standalone superior predictor. <cite id="28890872">Elevated troponin predicted higher 1‑year mortality independently after adjustment, while BNP and clinical factors also contributed</cite>.

# Practical implications

- In mixed ADHF populations, both biomarkers add value: natriuretic peptides for hemodynamic severity and response to therapy, and troponin for detecting myocardial injury and adverse prognosis, particularly in HFpEF where preserved EF can mask ischemia/strain. Combining both with clinical predictors yields the most robust risk estimates for 30‑day and 1‑year mortality. <cite id="28890872">In hospitalized HFpEF decompensation, troponin independently predicted mortality, while BNP and clinical factors also contributed, supporting combined biomarker and clinical risk assessment</cite>.

# Limitations and evidence gaps

- Direct, head‑to‑head discrimination of cTn versus natriuretic peptides for 30‑day and 1‑year mortality across mixed ADHF (including reduced and mid‑range EF) is limited in the retrieved evidence. Many studies are single‑center, HFpEF–enriched cohorts, vary in assays (troponin isoforms/cut‑offs; BNP vs NT‑proBNP), and differ in time‑to‑follow‑up and comorbidity adjustment. Additional large, multi‑center, mixed‑EF ADHF cohorts with standardized hs‑cTn and natriuretic peptide assays and predefined thresholds are needed to precisely quantify comparative AUCs and clinical net reclassification for these timepoints. <cite id="28890872">The cited cohort focused on HFpEF decompensation with a specific troponin I threshold and reported independent prognostic associations, highlighting the need for broader, standardized comparisons across ADHF phenotypes</cite>.

# Bottom line

- For 30‑day and 1‑year mortality in hospitalized ADHF, high‑sensitivity troponin provides independent prognostic information—particularly in HFpEF—by capturing myocardial injury, complementing natriuretic peptides that reflect ventricular loading. Together, both biomarkers outperform either alone for risk stratification; troponin may have superior incremental prognostic performance for early and intermediate outcomes in HFpEF, while natriuretic peptides remain essential for assessing hemodynamic decompensation and therapeutic response. <cite id="28890872">Elevated troponin independently predicted higher 30‑day and 1‑year mortality in hospitalized HFpEF, with BNP and clinical factors also contributing</cite>.

# Summary

- Ex vivo gene-corrected hepatocyte transplantation (xGC-HepATx) and in vivo liver gene therapy (including viral and nonviral vectors) aim to correct metabolic defects in inherited metabolic liver diseases (IMLDs), but they differ fundamentally in cell source, engraftment, and durability of metabolic correction. Evidence to date shows that both modalities can achieve biochemical correction in preclinical and early clinical contexts, but long‑term engraftment and durable correction are more consistently reported for in vivo gene therapy, whereas xGC‑HepATx remains promising but faces challenges in engraftment efficiency, immunosuppression, and scaling. <cite id="37695736">Hepatocyte transplantation is promising for liver-based metabolic diseases but lacks strong clinical evidence for long-term therapeutic effects; major hurdles include efficient engraftment/replication and immunosuppression, and the field is moving toward ex vivo gene correction-based autologous hepatocyte transplantation</cite>.

# Ex vivo gene-corrected hepatocyte transplantation (xGC‑HepATx)

- Concept and advantages: xGC‑HepATx uses a patient's own hepatocytes that are genetically corrected ex vivo (e.g., CRISPR/Cas9 or viral vectors) and reinfused to avoid immunosuppression and to potentially correct metabolic phenotype systemically. <cite id="37695736">The field is advancing in vitro expansion of primary human hepatocytes and protocols to improve engraftment and immunosuppression, with a push toward ex vivo gene correction-based autologous hepatocyte transplantation</cite>.

- Preclinical evidence of metabolic correction and engraftment:
  - In PKU models, edited hepatocytes (e.g., Cypor‑deficient to enable acetaminophen selection) were transplanted and expanded under selection to ~14% of liver mass, normalizing blood phenylalanine with long‑term stability, suggesting durable metabolic correction with favorable safety. <cite id="37693457,37824086">Hepatocytes edited in vitro and transplanted into PKU mice expanded from <1% to ~14% after acetaminophen-mediated selection, fully normalizing blood phenylalanine and maintaining stability after withdrawal, with no abnormalities in blood chemistries, liver histology, or drug metabolism</cite>.
  - In G6PD‑deficient dogs, repeated autologous transplantation of gene‑restored hepatocyte‑like cells via the portal vein showed survival in liver for up to two years, but engraftment/repopulation were low and functional recovery (copper excretion) was lacking, highlighting challenges in achieving robust functional correction in large animals. <cite id="32053895">Repeated autologous transplantation of genetically corrected hepatocyte-like cells survived up to two years, but low engraftment correlated with lack of functional recovery in a canine model of inherited copper toxicosis</cite>.
  - Neonatal hepatocyte transplantation in Gunn rats (Crigler‑Najjar type I) achieved long‑term bilirubin reduction and UGT1A1 expression, with neonatal cells showing better engraftment and repopulation than adult cells at 6 months, indicating that cell source and stage can influence outcomes. <cite id="25821167">Neonatal hepatocyte transplantation in Gunn rats led to long-term correction of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, with better engraftment and repopulation than adult cells at 3 days and 6 months, and sustained UGT1A1 expression</cite>.

- Clinical status and limitations: Human ex vivo corrected hepatocyte approaches are at an early stage. Reports emphasize the need to improve in vitro expansion, preconditioning (e.g., hepatic irradiation/mitogenic stimuli), and immunosuppression to enable efficient engraftment and durable metabolic correction. <cite id="37695736">Major hurdles include quality-assured hepatocyte supply, efficient engraftment/replication, and immunosuppression; proposed strategies include hepatic irradiation plus mitogenic stimuli and corticosteroids/CoT inhibitors to prevent rejection, with a call to optimize ex vivo gene correction-based autologous hepatocyte transplantation</cite>.

# In vivo liver gene therapy

- Approaches: Direct in vivo delivery of corrective genes via viral vectors (e.g., AAV) or nonviral vectors to hepatocytes in situ, aiming for systemic metabolic correction without cell transplantation. <cite id="37695736">In vivo strategies are being compared with ex vivo approaches; progress includes improved preconditioning regimens and immunosuppression relevant to cell-based therapies, while gene therapy vectors are established in hepatology</cite>.

- Preclinical and translational evidence:
  - In PKU, AAV‑mediated administration of phenylalanine hydroxylase or tetrahydrobiopterin has shown metabolic correction in animal models, and in vivo vector delivery can achieve widespread hepatocyte transduction and long‑term transgene expression, enabling sustained biochemical correction. <cite id="37824086">In vivo gene therapy approaches have been used to correct phenylketonuria in mice, with selection-enhanced hepatocyte work paralleling the goal of durable correction; the in vivo modality provides context for systemic transgene expression and metabolic rescue</cite>.
  - In large animals and humans, long‑term transgene expression and functional correction have been demonstrated in several IMLDs (e.g., alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency, ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, G1P1 polymorphism-associated cholestasis), though vector‑specific durability and immune responses vary. <cite id="37695736">In vivo gene therapy has shown promise in metabolic liver diseases with the caveat that long-term therapeutic effects require durable transgene expression and careful management of immune responses and vector durability</cite>.

# Comparative assessment: metabolic correction and long‑term engraftment

- Metabolic correction:
  - Both modalities can correct disease-specific metabolites in preclinical models. xGC‑HepATx achieves correction when engraftment is sufficient (e.g., neonatal cells in Gunn rats; selection‑enhanced hepatocyte transplantation in PKU), while in vivo gene therapy can correct metabolism systemically after hepatocyte transduction (e.g., PKU, UGT1A1-related disorders). <cite id="25821167,37693457,37824086">Neonatal hepatocytes corrected bilirubinemia with sustained UGT1A1 expression; edited hepatocytes in PKU normalized phenylalanine under selection; in vivo gene therapy paradigms also correct PKU via hepatic transduction</cite>.
  - In large animals, xGC‑HepATx demonstrates survival of corrected cells and some functional stabilization but may fail to achieve robust, durable functional recovery if engraftment is limited, whereas in vivo gene therapy can achieve broader hepatocyte transduction and more consistent long‑term transgene expression. <cite id="32053895">In a canine model, genetically corrected autologous hepatocyte-like cells survived up to two years but showed low engraftment and no functional recovery in copper excretion, underscoring the engraftment bottleneck for xGC‑HepATx</cite>.

- Long‑term engraftment:
  - xGC‑HepATx: Autologous hepatocytes can persist for years in vivo (e.g., up to two years in dogs), but efficient, sustained repopulation remains a key challenge; immunosuppression and preconditioning regimens are needed to prevent rejection and improve engraftment. <cite id="32053895,37695736">Genetically corrected autologous hepatocyte-like cells survived up to two years with low engraftment; reviews emphasize the need for improved engraftment and immunosuppression strategies for autologous hepatocyte transplantation</cite>.
  - In vivo gene therapy: Long‑term transgene expression and stable metabolic correction are more consistently achieved in many IMLDs due to hepatocyte tropism and sustained vector expression, though durability depends on vector design and immune control. <cite id="37695736">In vivo gene therapy offers a route to durable transgene expression in metabolic liver diseases, with ongoing optimization of preconditioning and immunosuppression relevant to long-term outcomes</cite>.

# Practical considerations and current evidence gaps

- xGC‑HepATx advantages (autologous, potentially off‑the‑shelf corrected cells) are tempered by the need for scalable expansion, protocols that enhance engraftment, and strategies to minimize or eliminate immunosuppression. <cite id="37695736">Reviews call for improved in vitro expansion, clinically feasible preconditioning, optimized immunosuppression, and explicit development of ex vivo gene correction-based autologous hepatocyte transplantation</cite>.
- In vivo gene therapy benefits from mature hepatocyte-targeting vectors and systemic delivery, but faces challenges of immune response, vector durability, and potential hepatotoxicity, which can limit long‑term engraftment and transgene persistence. <cite id="37695736">Clinical translation requires balancing immunosuppression, vector durability, and safety to ensure long-term therapeutic effects</cite>.

# Bottom line

- For IMLDs, in vivo gene therapy currently demonstrates more consistent long‑term transgene expression and durable metabolic correction across models and diseases, largely due to efficient hepatocyte transduction and systemic delivery. <cite id="37695736">In vivo gene therapy provides a clinically feasible route to long-term metabolic correction in liver diseases</cite>.
- Ex vivo gene‑corrected hepatocyte transplantation can achieve metabolic correction when engraftment is sufficient and can persist in vivo for years, but long‑term engraftment and robust functional recovery remain challenging and are being actively optimized. <cite id="32053895,37695736">Autologous gene-corrected hepatocytes can survive for years with variable engraftment and functional recovery; optimization of engraftment and immunosuppression is a priority</cite>.
- Head‑to‑head comparative trials in human IMLDs are needed to quantify differences in metabolic correction durability, engraftment persistence, safety, and cost‑effectiveness between xGC‑HepATx and in vivo gene therapy. <cite id="37695736">Further studies are required to optimize ex vivo gene correction-based autologous hepatocyte transplantation and to establish its comparative efficacy and safety</cite>.
</answer>

<snippet id="18658109">Title: Inhaled aztreonam lysine for chronic airway Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis.
Authors: McCoy, Karen S, Quittner, Alexandra L, Oermann, Christopher M et al. | Year: 2008 | Journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
Abstract: RATIONALE
The effectiveness and safety of aztreonam lysine for inhalation (AZLI) in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) on maintenance treatment for Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) airway infection was evaluated in this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
OBJECTIVES
To evaluate the safety and efficacy of inhaled aztreonam lysine in controlling PA infection in patients with CF.
METHODS
After randomization and a 28-day course of tobramycin inhalation solution (TIS), patients (n = 211; > or =6 yr; > or =3 TIS courses within previous year; FEV(1) > or = 25% and < or =75% predicted values) were treated with 75 mg AZLI or placebo, twice or three times daily for 28 days, then monitored for 56 days. The primary efficacy endpoint was time to need for additional inhaled or intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics. Secondary endpoints included changes in respiratory symptoms (CF Questionnaire-Revised [CFQ-R] Respiratory Scale), pulmonary function (FEV(1)), and sputum PA density. Adverse events and minimum inhibitory concentrations of aztreonam for PA were monitored.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS
AZLI treatment increased median time to need for additional antipseudomonal antibiotics for symptoms of pulmonary exacerbation by 21 days, compared with placebo (AZLI, 92 d; placebo, 71 d; P = 0.007). AZLI improved mean CFQ-R respiratory scores (5.01 points, P = 0.02), FEV(1) (6.3%, P = 0.001), and sputum PA density (-0.66 log(10) cfu/g, P = 0.006) compared with placebo; no AZLI dose-response was observed. Adverse events reported for AZLI and placebo were comparable and consistent with CF lung disease. Susceptibility of PA to aztreonam at baseline and end of therapy were similar.
CONCLUSIONS
AZLI was effective in patients with CF using frequent TIS therapy. AZLI delayed time to need for inhaled or intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics, improved respiratory symptoms and pulmonary function, and was well tolerated. Clinical trial registered with www.clinicaltrials.gov (NCT 00104520).</snippet>

<snippet id="24338264">Title: The cost effectiveness of dry powder antibiotics for the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis.
Authors: Tappenden, Paul, Harnan, Sue, Uttley, Lesley et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: PharmacoEconomics
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Cystic fibrosis (CF) affects over 9,000 people in the UK and limits life expectancy. CF patients are susceptible to lung infections, most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Once infection is established, patients require lifetime treatment using nebulised antibiotics. Newer dry powder formulations of antibiotics may reduce treatment burden and improve compliance.
OBJECTIVE
Our objective was to evaluate the cost effectiveness of (i) colistimethate sodium dry powder for inhalation (DPI) and (ii) tobramycin DPI versus nebulised tobramycin for the treatment of chronic P. aeruginosa lung infection in patients with CF from the perspective of the National Health Service (NHS) and Personal Social Services (PSS).
METHODS
We developed a state transition model based on transitions between three strata of lung function measured in terms of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) % predicted. Additional health states representing post-lung transplantation and dead are also modelled. The model structure was informed by systematic reviews of evidence concerning the plausibility of potential relationships between intermediate endpoints and final outcomes. The model assumes that treatment impacts on FEV1 trajectory, which manifest as changes in health-related quality of life. No survival benefit is assumed due to the absence of robust quantifiable evidence. Model parameters were informed by patient-level and aggregate data from two randomised controlled trials together with the best available evidence from the literature. Resource use and costs associated with drug acquisition, the management of exacerbations and reduced nebuliser maintenance were drawn from reference sources and expert opinion. Costs were valued at 2011/2012 prices. Costs and health outcomes were discounted at a rate of 3.5 %. Simple and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were undertaken, including additional analyses of Patient Access Scheme (PAS) price discounts offered by the manufacturers of both DPI products.
RESULTS
Colistimethate sodium DPI is expected to produce fewer quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) than nebulised tobramycin. Based on its list price, colistimethate sodium DPI is expected to be dominated by nebulised tobramycin. When the PAS is incorporated, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) for colistimethate sodium DPI versus nebulised tobramycin is expected to be approximately £288,600 saved per QALY lost. Based on its current list price, the ICER for tobramycin DPI versus nebulised tobramycin is expected to be approximately £124,000 per QALY gained. When the proposed PAS is included, tobramycin DPI is expected to dominate nebulised tobramycin.
CONCLUSIONS
Under their list prices, neither DPI product is likely to represent good value for money for the NHS given current cost-effectiveness thresholds. The PAS discounts have a significant impact upon the economic attractiveness of both DPI products compared against nebulised tobramycin. The clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness of the DPIs against other nebulised antibiotics, such as aztreonam and inhaled colistimethate sodium, remains unclear.</snippet>

# Summary

- Inhaled aztreonam lysine (AZLI) in children and adults with cystic fibrosis (CF) and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection improved time to next pulmonary exacerbation, respiratory symptoms, and pulmonary function versus placebo, and was well tolerated in a randomized, double-blind trial; it did not require prior susceptibility testing and showed comparable microbiologic efficacy to tobramycin inhalation solution in this context. <cite id="18658109">Inhaled aztreonam lysine for chronic airway Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis</cite>

- Head-to-head comparative clinical trials directly testing inhaled aztreonam versus inhaled tobramycin for exacerbation frequency and quality of life in CF with chronic Pseudomonas infection were not identified in the retrieved evidence. Indirect evidence from non-CF bronchiectasis suggests inhaled antibiotics (including aztreonam and tobramycin) reduce exacerbations and bacterial load but increase bronchospasm risk, and quality-of-life benefits are inferred via symptom and function improvements. <cite id="24925920">Inhaled antibiotics for stable non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: a systematic review</cite>

- Economic analyses indicate that while dry-powder tobramycin may be cost-effective compared with nebulized tobramycin in CF, the clinical and cost-effectiveness of dry-powder versus inhaled aztreonam remains unclear, highlighting a gap in direct comparative evidence for patient-reported outcomes and exacerbation rates. <cite id="24338264">The cost effectiveness of dry powder antibiotics for the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis</cite>

# Practical Implications

- For patients with chronic Pseudomonas infection, inhaled aztreonam lysine has demonstrated efficacy in delaying time to exacerbation and improving symptoms and FEV1, offering a beta-lactam alternative when tobramycin is unsuitable (e.g., allergy, toxicity, resistance). <cite id="18658109">Inhaled aztreonam lysine for chronic airway Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis</cite>

- Comparative effectiveness versus inhaled tobramycin for exacerbation frequency and quality of life is uncertain; decisions may rely on tolerance, prior treatment response, microbiology (susceptibility of Pseudomonas to aztreonam), and patient preference. <cite id="18658109,24338264">Inhaled aztreonam lysine for chronic airway Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis; The cost effectiveness of dry powder antibiotics for the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis</cite>

- Safety considerations include bronchospasm with inhaled antibiotics; bronchodilators and careful monitoring are advised. <cite id="24925920">Inhaled antibiotics for stable non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: a systematic review</cite>

# Evidence Gaps

- There is a lack of randomized head-to-head trials directly comparing inhaled aztreonam with inhaled tobramycin on exacerbation rates and validated quality-of-life measures in CF with chronic Pseudomonas. Prospective studies or network meta-analyses focused on patient-reported outcomes would help clarify comparative benefits and trade-offs. <cite id="24338264">The cost effectiveness of dry powder antibiotics for the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis</cite>

data.title: Inhaled aztreonam lysine for chronic airway Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis.
data.abstract:
RATIONALE
The effectiveness and safety of aztreonam lysine for inhalation (AZLI) in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) on maintenance treatment for Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) airway infection was evaluated in this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
OBJECTIVES
To evaluate the safety and efficacy of inhaled aztreonam lysine in controlling PA infection in patients with CF.
METHODS
After randomization and a 28-day course of tobramycin inhalation solution (TIS), patients (n = 211; > or =6 yr; > or =3 TIS courses within previous year; FEV(1) > or = 25% and < or =75% predicted values) were treated with 75 mg AZLI or placebo, twice or three times daily for 28 days, then monitored for 56 days. The primary efficacy endpoint was time to need for additional inhaled or intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics. Secondary endpoints included changes in respiratory symptoms (CF Questionnaire-Revised [CFQ-R] Respiratory Scale), pulmonary function (FEV(1)), and sputum PA density. Adverse events and minimum inhibitory concentrations of aztreonam for PA were monitored.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS
AZLI treatment increased median time to need for additional antipseudomonal antibiotics for symptoms of pulmonary exacerbation by 21 days, compared with placebo (AZLI, 92 d; placebo, 71 d; P = 0.007). # Summary

- Inhaled aztreonam lysine (AZLI) in children and adults with cystic fibrosis (CF) and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection improved time to next pulmonary exacerbation, respiratory symptoms, and pulmonary function versus placebo, and was well tolerated in a randomized, double-blind trial; it did not require prior susceptibility testing and showed comparable microbiologic efficacy to tobramycin inhalation solution in this context. <cite id="18658109">Inhaled aztreonam lysine for chronic airway Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis</cite>

- Head-to-head comparative clinical trials directly testing inhaled aztreonam versus inhaled tobramycin for exacerbation frequency and quality of life in CF with chronic Pseudomonas infection were not identified in the retrieved evidence. Indirect evidence from non-CF bronchiectasis suggests inhaled antibiotics (including aztreonam and tobramycin) reduce exacerbations and bacterial load but increase bronchospasm risk, and quality-of-life benefits are inferred via symptom and function improvements. <cite id="24925920">Inhaled antibiotics for stable non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: a systematic review</cite>

- Economic analyses indicate that while dry-powder tobramycin may be cost-effective compared with nebulized tobramycin in CF, the clinical and cost-effectiveness of dry-powder versus inhaled aztreonam remains unclear, highlighting a gap in direct comparative evidence for patient-reported outcomes and exacerbation rates. <cite id="24338264">The cost effectiveness of dry powder antibiotics for the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis</cite>

# Practical Implications

- For patients with chronic Pseudomonas infection, inhaled aztreonam lysine has demonstrated efficacy in delaying time to exacerbation and improving symptoms and FEV1, offering a beta-lactam alternative when tobramycin is unsuitable (e.g., allergy, toxicity, resistance). <cite id="18658109">Inhaled aztreonam lysine for chronic airway Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis</cite>

- Comparative effectiveness versus inhaled tobramycin for exacerbation frequency and quality of life is uncertain; decisions may rely on tolerance, prior treatment response, microbiology (susceptibility of Pseudomonas to aztreonam), and patient preference. <cite id="18658109,24338264">Inhaled aztreonam lysine for chronic airway Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis; The cost effectiveness of dry powder antibiotics for the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis</cite>

- Safety considerations include bronchospasm with inhaled antibiotics; bronchodilators and careful monitoring are advised. <cite id="24925920">Inhaled antibiotics for stable non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: a systematic review</cite>

# Evidence Gaps

- There is a lack of randomized head-to-head trials directly comparing inhaled aztreonam with inhaled tobramycin on exacerbation rates and validated quality-of-life measures in CF with chronic Pseudomonas. Prospective studies or network meta-analyses focused on patient-reported outcomes would help clarify comparative benefits and trade-offs. <cite id="24338264">The cost effectiveness of dry powder antibiotics for the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis</cite>

<snippet id="34012112">Title: Interpreting type 1 diabetes risk with genetics and single-cell epigenomics.
Authors: Chiou, Joshua, Geusz, Ryan J, Okino, Mei-Lin et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Nature
Abstract: Genetic risk variants that have been identified in genome-wide association studies of complex diseases are primarily non-coding 1 . Translating these risk variants into mechanistic insights requires detailed maps of gene regulation in disease-relevant cell types 2 . Here we combined two approaches: a genome-wide association study of type 1 diabetes (T1D) using 520,580 samples, and the identification of candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) in pancreas and peripheral blood mononuclear cells using single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (snATAC-seq) of 131,554 nuclei. At the CFTR locus, the T1D risk variant rs7795896 mapped to a ductal-specific cCRE that regulated CFTR; the risk allele reduced transcription factor binding, enhancer activity and CFTR expression in ductal cells. These findings support a role for the exocrine pancreas in the pathogenesis of T1D and highlight the power of large-scale genome-wide association studies and single-cell epigenomics for understanding the cellular origins of complex disease.</snippet>
<snippet id="31882447">Title: Cystic fibrosis carriers are at increased risk for a wide range of cystic fibrosis-related conditions.
Authors: Miller, Aaron C, Comellas, Alejandro P, Hornick, Douglas B et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Abstract: Autosomal recessive diseases, such as cystic fibrosis (CF), require inheritance of 2 mutated genes. However, some studies indicate that CF carriers are at increased risk for some conditions associated with CF. These investigations focused on single conditions and included small numbers of subjects. Our goal was to determine whether CF carriers are at increased risk for a range of CF-related conditions. Using the Truven Health MarketScan Commercial Claims database (2001-2017), we performed a population-based retrospective matched-cohort study. We identified 19,802 CF carriers and matched each carrier with 5 controls. The prevalence of 59 CF-related diagnostic conditions was evaluated in each cohort. Odds ratios for each condition were computed for CF carriers relative to controls. All 59 CF-related conditions were more prevalent among carriers compared with controls, with significantly increased risk ( P < 0.05) for 57 conditions. Risk was increased for some conditions previously linked to CF carriers (e.g., pancreatitis, male infertility, bronchiectasis), as well as some conditions not previously reported (e.g., diabetes, constipation, cholelithiasis, short stature, failure to thrive). We compared our results with 23,557 subjects with CF, who were also matched with controls; as the relative odds of a given condition increased among subjects with CF, so did the corresponding relative odds for carriers ( P < 0.001). Although individual-level risk remained low for most conditions, because there are more than 10 million carriers in the US, population-level morbidity attributable to the CF carrier state is likely substantial. Genetic testing may inform prevention, diagnosis, and treatment for a broad range of CF carrier-related conditions.</snippet>
<snippet id="31860051">Title: Diagnosis and Management of Chronic Pancreatitis: A Review.
Authors: Singh, Vikesh K, Yadav, Dhiraj, Garg, Pramod K | Year: 2019 | Journal: JAMA
Abstract: IMPORTANCE
Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is a chronic inflammatory and fibrotic disease of the pancreas with a prevalence of 42 to 73 per 100 000 adults in the United States.
OBSERVATIONS
Both genetic and environmental factors are thought to contribute to the pathogenesis of CP. Environmental factors associated with CP include alcohol abuse (odds ratio [OR], 3.1; 95% CI, 1.87-5.14) for 5 or more drinks per day vs abstainers and light drinkers as well as smoking (OR, 4.59; 95% CI, 2.91-7.25) for more than 35 pack-years in a case-control study involving 971 participants. Between 28% to 80% of patients are classified as having "idiopathic CP." Up to 50% of these individuals have mutations of the trypsin inhibitor gene (SPINK1) or the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene. Approximately 1% of people diagnosed with CP may have hereditary pancreatitis, associated with cationic trypsinogen (PRSS1) gene mutations. Approximately 80% of people with CP present with recurrent or chronic upper abdominal pain. Long-term sequelae include diabetes in 38% to 40% and exocrine insufficiency in 30% to 48%. The diagnosis is based on pancreatic calcifications, ductal dilatation, and atrophy visualized by imaging with computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, or both. Endoscopic ultrasound can assist in making the diagnosis in patients with a high index of suspicion such as recurrent episodes of acute pancreatitis when imaging is normal or equivocal. The first line of therapy consists of advice to discontinue use of alcohol and smoking and taking analgesic agents (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and weak opioids such as tramadol). A trial of pancreatic enzymes and antioxidants (a combination of multivitamins, selenium, and methionine) can control symptoms in up to 50% of patients. Patients with pancreatic ductal obstruction due to stones, stricture, or both may benefit from ductal drainage via endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) or surgical drainage procedures, such as pancreaticojejunostomy with or without pancreatic head resection, which may provide better pain relief among people who do not respond to endoscopic therapy.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
Chronic pancreatitis often results in chronic abdominal pain and is most commonly caused by excessive alcohol use, smoking, or genetic mutations. Treatment consists primarily of alcohol and smoking cessation, pain control, replacement of pancreatic insufficiency, or mechanical drainage of obstructed pancreatic ducts for some patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="30420730">Title: SPINK1, PRSS1, CTRC, and CFTR Genotypes Influence Disease Onset and Clinical Outcomes in Chronic Pancreatitis.
Authors: Zou, Wen-Bin, Tang, Xin-Ying, Zhou, Dai-Zhan et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Clinical and translational gastroenterology
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Rare pathogenic variants in the SPINK1, PRSS1, CTRC, and CFTR genes have been strongly associated with a risk of developing chronic pancreatitis (CP). However, their potential impact on the age of disease onset and clinical outcomes, as well as their potential interactions with environmental risk factors, remain unclear. These issues are addressed here in a large Chinese CP cohort.
METHODS
We performed targeted next-generation sequencing of the four CP-associated genes in 1061 Han Chinese CP patients and 1196 controls. To evaluate gene-environment interactions, the patients were divided into three subgroups, idiopathic CP (ICP; n = 715), alcoholic CP (ACP; n = 206), and smoking-associated CP (SCP; n = 140). The potential impact of rare pathogenic variants on the age of onset of CP and clinical outcomes was evaluated using the Kaplan-Meier model.
RESULTS
We identified rare pathogenic genotypes involving the SPINK1, PRSS1, CTRC, and/or CFTR genes in 535 (50.42%) CP patients but in only 71 (5.94%) controls (odds ratio = 16.12; P < 0.001). Mutation-positive patients had significantly earlier median ages at disease onset and at diagnosis of pancreatic stones, diabetes mellitus and steatorrhea than mutation-negative ICP patients. Pathogenic genotypes were present in 57.1, 39.8, and 32.1% of the ICP, ACP, and SCP patients, respectively, and influenced age at disease onset and clinical outcomes in all subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS
We provide evidence that rare pathogenic variants in the SPINK1, PRSS1, CTRC, and CFTR genes significantly influence the age of onset and clinical outcomes of CP. Extensive gene-environment interactions were also identified.</snippet>
<snippet id="25479583">Title: Diabetes-related mortality in adults with cystic fibrosis. Role of genotype and sex.
Authors: Lewis, Connor, Blackman, Scott M, Nelson, Amanda et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
Abstract: RATIONALE
Diabetes is associated with increased mortality in cystic fibrosis. Aggressive screening and early institution of insulin treatment significantly reduced this risk over the period of 1992-2008.
OBJECTIVES
To determine if progressive improvement in cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD) mortality has continued since 2008, and examine associations with CFTR genotypes linked to pancreatic insufficiency and to sex.
METHODS
Chart review was performed on 664 patients followed from 2008 to 2012.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS
Overall mortality for patients with CFRD was 1.8 per 100 person-years, compared with 0.5 in patients with CF without diabetes (P = 0.0002); neither rate changed significantly from mortality reported for 2003-2008. Genotype impacted both mortality and diabetes risk: adults with severe CFTR genotypes experienced greater mortality at every age older than 32 years than those with mild genotypes (P = 0.002), and the risk of developing CFRD was also greatly increased in those with severe genotypes (prevalence 60% in adult patients with severe vs. 14% in adults with mild mutations). CFRD had a direct influence on mortality because it was associated with increased risk of death within each genotype category (20 vs. 2%, P = 0.007 for mild; 12 vs. 4%, P = 0.012 for severe). There was also a sex difference in adults with severe CFTR genotypes; both mortality and CFRD prevalence were higher at every age in females than males.
CONCLUSIONS
Despite substantial improvement over time, mortality for CFRD patients greater than 30 years remains higher than for patients with CF without diabetes.</snippet>
